questions.stem: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness, and syncopal attacks. On examination, irregularly irregular pulse is seen. What will be seen on JVP?
questions.stemHtml: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness, and syncopal attacks. On examination, irregularly irregular pulse is seen. What will be seen on JVP?
questions.solution: 2a8b2">irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation (AF), which is common in chronic alcoholics (so-called holiday heart syndrome ). In AF, the atria do not contract effectively → no coordinated atrial systole → no a wave is produced in the jugular venous pulse (JVP). Therefore, the finding will be absent a wave. Jugular Venous Pulse (JVP) reflects right atrial pressure changes during the cardiac cycle. The a wave corresponds to atrial contraction (just before S1). In AF, there is complete loss of organized atrial contraction → a wave disappears. Chronic alcoholics are prone to AF due to atrial dilation, electrolyte imbalance, and direct myocardial effects. Atrial fibrillation: Feature Details ECG Irregularly irregular RR intervals, absent P waves, fibrillatory baseline Causes Hypertension, valvular heart disease (esp. mitral), alcohol (holiday heart), thyrotoxicosis Complications Stroke, heart failure, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy Management Rate control (β-blockers, CCBs), rhythm control (amiodarone, cardioversion), anticoagulation (CHA₂DS₂-VASc score) JVP Waveform: Positive waves in JVP: a, c and v a wave - Atrium Contraction (Lat Rapid Filling Phase) c wave - Cusp bulging (tricuspid valve cusp bulging towards the atrium) v wave - Venous return Negative waves in JVP: x wave - Atrium relaxation x' wave - Tricuspid valve pulling towards the ventricle y descend - Opening of tricuspid valve JVP finding Cause Absent a wave Atrial fibrillation Large a wave Tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension Cannon a wave Complete heart block, VT (atria contracting against closed tricuspid valve) Steep y descent Constrictive pericarditis Incorrect Options: Large a wave (Option B) – Seen when the right atrium contracts against high resistance, e.g., tricuspid stenosis or pulmonary hypertension. Canon a wave (Option C) – Occurs when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve, e.g., complete heart block, VT. Steep y descent (Option D) – Seen in constrictive pericarditis and severe tricuspid regurgitation. @Neet_pg_bot

Management

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female with a previous history of rheumatic fever. Examination shows a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur is having which of the following valvular heart disease?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old female with a previous history of rheumatic fever. Examination shows a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur is having which of the following valvular heart disease?
questions.solution: bc2b21e">Stenosis (MS): Explanation: The patient has a history of rheumatic fever and presents with a loud S1 and mid-diastolic murmur, which are classic findings of mitral stenosis. Rheumatic fever is the most common cause of MS worldwide. Mitral stenosis results from thickening and fusion of the mitral valve leaflets, most often due to rheumatic heart disease. The loud S1 occurs because the stiff valve closes forcefully, and the mid-diastolic murmur is due to turbulent flow across the narrowed mitral orifice during diastole. Other features may include an opening snap and signs of pulmonary congestion. Mitral stenosis: Cause: Rheumatic fever (most common), congenital, calcific degeneration (elderly). Pathophysiology: Narrowed mitral orifice → ↑ left atrial pressure → pulmonary venous hypertension → right heart strain. Clinical features: Dyspnea, orthopnea, hemoptysis, atrial fibrillation. Auscultation: Loud S1, opening snap after S2, low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex (best heard with the patient in the left lateral position). Complications: Pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, thromboembolism. Treatment: Medical (diuretics, rate control for AF) or surgical (percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy, valve replacement). Incorrect Options: Tricuspid Stenosis (TS) (Option A) – Mid-diastolic murmur increases with inspiration; usually occurs with MS but isolated TS is rare. Mitral Regurgitation (MR) (Option B) – Produces a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, not a mid-diastolic murmur. Aortic Regurgitation (AR) (Option D) – Produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, not associated with loud S1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents to the ER with central chest pain. He has a past medical history of heart disease. ECG is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents to the ER with central chest pain. He has a past medical history of heart disease. ECG is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: > ST-segment elevation: Anterior leads: V2–V4 Lateral leads: I, aVL, V5, V6 Reciprocal ST-segment depression: leads III and aVF (inferior leads) Interpretation: This combination indicates acute injury involving both the anterior wall (supplied by the LAD) and the lateral wall (supplied by the LCX or diagonal branches of LAD) — hence, anterolateral MI. Reciprocal changes (ST depression in inferior leads) strengthen the diagnosis of acute MI and help differentiate from pericarditis. MI location vs. ECG leads MI Location Leads with ST Elevation Likely Artery Anterior V1–V4 LAD Lateral I, aVL, V5, V6 LCX or diagonal branch Anterolateral V2–V6, I, aVL LAD + LCX/diagonal branch Inferior II, III, aVF RCA or LCX Inferolateral II, III, aVF, I, aVL, V5, V6 RCA + LCX Posterior V7–V9 (or tall R in V1–V2) RCA or LCX Incorrect Options: Inferolateral MI (Option B): Inferolateral MI would have ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) plus lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). Here, inferior leads show ST depression, not elevation → rules out this option. Acute pericarditis (Option C): Pericarditis usually has diffuse ST elevation across almost all leads without reciprocal ST depression (except in aVR/V1) and PR segment depression. This ECG shows localized ST elevation with clear reciprocal changes — typical of MI, not pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis (Option D): Constrictive pericarditis is a chronic condition; ECG may show low voltage QRS or nonspecific changes, not acute ST elevation patterns. It presents with signs like Kussmaul’s sign, pericardial knock, and right heart failure — not acute chest pain + STEMI pattern. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient after MI develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia. His BP is 120/85 mm Hg. ECG is given below. Best management?
questions.stemHtml: A patient after MI develops a broad QRS complex tachycardia. His BP is 120/85 mm Hg. ECG is given below. Best management?
questions.solution: rong> Broad QRS (>120 ms) Regular tachycardia Monomorphic appearance Post-MI patient → high risk of ventricular tachycardia (VT) Diagnosis: Sustained monomorphic VT Step 2: Assessing stability BP = 120/85 mm Hg → patient is hemodynamically stable (no shock, syncope, severe hypotension, or heart failure). In stable VT, first-line pharmacologic management = IV amiodarone (or procainamide in some guidelines). Class III antiarrhythmic that prolongs repolarisation and suppresses ventricular ectopy. Preferred in structural heart disease post-MI because other agents (like some beta-blockers) may worsen VT in the acute setting. Stable vs. unstable broad complex tachycardia (VT) Status First-line management Stable VT IV amiodarone (or procainamide) Unstable VT Immediate synchronized DC cardioversion Pulseless VT / VF Immediate defibrillation + CPR Incorrect Options: Labetalol IV (Option B): Labetalol is an alpha- and beta-blocker used for hypertension, not for acute VT management. Giving it here will not terminate VT and can worsen instability. Metoprolol IV (Option C): While beta-blockers are used post-MI for arrhythmia prevention, they are not the first choice for terminating sustained VT in the acute phase. Risk of worsening hypotension or bradyarrhythmia once VT resolves. Nitroglycerin IV (Option D) Used for angina or heart failure due to ischemia. Has no role in terminating VT. May cause hypotension in this context. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Labetalol is an alpha- and beta-blocker used for hypertension, not for acute VT management.

questions.stem: A study was conducted among nursing staff to analyze the time spent on different aspects of patient care, such as bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending the doctor’s rounds, blood sampling, and drug administration. Which of the following management techniques is most appropriate for this type of analysis?
questions.stemHtml: A study was conducted among nursing staff to analyze the time spent on different aspects of patient care, such as bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending the doctor’s rounds, blood sampling, and drug administration. Which of the following management techniques is most appropriate for this type of analysis?
questions.solution: strong>Explanation: The study in the question focuses on estimating how much time nursing staff spend on various activities across the day, but not by continuously timing each task from start to finish. Work Sampling is the appropriate method here because it involves taking observations at random intervals to determine the proportion of time spent on different activities. Work Sampling: Definition: A statistical technique for determining the proportion of time spent on various activities by making observations at random intervals. Purpose: Assess workload distribution. Identify major time-consuming activities. Provide data for staffing and scheduling decisions. Applications in Healthcare: Studying nurse-patient interaction time. Determining how much time doctors spend in direct patient care vs. paperwork. Evaluating efficiency in diagnostic labs. Critical Path Method (Option A) : Project management technique for scheduling dependent tasks; not for estimating activity time proportions. System Analysis (Option B): Studies entire systems and processes; too broad for specific activity-time proportion studies. Time and Motion Study (Option D): Continuous observation of each step of a task; gives detailed task timings but is more intrusive and detailed than required for this study. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair, and dry skin. Diagnosis is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Which antibody is seen in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with weight gain, thinning of hair, and dry skin. Diagnosis is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Which antibody is seen in this case?
questions.solution: class="customMeta" data-dictid="df0e1364a11692777200ed67550c12">thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas, and it is strongly associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies. These antibodies cause autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland. Anti-TPO antibodies target the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, which is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis (oxidation and iodination of iodine, coupling of iodotyrosines). Their presence confirms autoimmune thyroid disease, especially Hashimoto’s. Other antibodies, like anti-thyroglobulin, may also be present but anti-TPO has the highest diagnostic relevance. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis: AKA Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis. Epidemiology: More common in women, especially middle-aged. Pathogenesis: Autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) → chronic inflammation → fibrosis → hypothyroidism. Clinical features: Weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair thinning, constipation, menstrual irregularities. Lab findings: High TSH, low free T4, positive anti-TPO antibodies. Histopathology : Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration Formation of germinal centers Hurthle cells (large oxyphilic epithelial cells with granular cytoplasm) replacing follicular epithelium Atrophic thyroid follicles with dense fibrosis in late stages Treatment: Lifelong levothyroxine replacement. Complications: Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma. Incorrect Options: Anti TSH (Option B) – Not seen in Hashimoto’s; would interfere with TSH action, not a diagnostic marker. Anti TBG (Option C) – Antibodies against thyroxine-binding globulin are rare and not relevant for Hashimoto’s diagnosis. Long-acting thyroid-stimulating antibody (Option D) – Seen in Graves’ disease, causes hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. @Neet_pg_bot

Anti-TPO antibodies target the enzyme thyroid peroxidase, which is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis (oxidation and iodination of iodine, coupling of iodotyrosines). Their presence confirms autoimmune thyroid disease, especially Hashimoto’s. Other antibodies, like anti-thyroglobulin, may also be present but anti-TPO has the highest diagnostic relevance.

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis:

  • AKA Chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis.
  • Epidemiology: More common in women, especially middle-aged.
  • Pathogenesis: Autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) → chronic inflammation → fibrosis → hypothyroidism.
  • Clinical features: Weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair thinning, constipation, menstrual irregularities.
  • Lab findings: High TSH, low free T4, positive anti-TPO antibodies.
  • Histopathology:
    • Diffuse lymphocytic infiltration
    • Formation of germinal centers
    • Hurthle cells (large oxyphilic epithelial cells with granular cytoplasm) replacing follicular epithelium
    • Atrophic thyroid follicles with dense fibrosis in late stages

  • Treatment: Lifelong levothyroxine replacement.
  • Complications: Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma.

Incorrect Options:

Anti TSH (Option B) – Not seen in Hashimoto’s; would interfere with TSH action, not a diagnostic marker.

Anti TBG (Option C) – Antibodies against thyroxine-binding globulin are rare and not relevant for Hashimoto’s diagnosis.

Long-acting thyroid-stimulating antibody (Option D) – Seen in Graves’ disease, causes hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: An RTA patient has received 4 packed RBC within a few hours. Which of the following will be seen?
questions.stemHtml: An RTA patient has received 4 packed RBC within a few hours. Which of the following will be seen?
questions.solution: s="customMeta" data-dictid="cbb73554631692777200444a9ea263">transfusion leads to citrate binding ionized calcium in the recipient’s blood, causing acute hypocalcemia. Citrate toxicity is more likely when large volumes of blood are transfused rapidly, as in massive transfusion protocols. The liver normally metabolizes citrate, but in shock or hypothermia this clearance is impaired. Clinical signs: Perioral numbness, paresthesia, muscle cramps, tetany, hypotension, and prolonged QT interval on ECG. Massive Blood Transfusion: Definition: Replacement of blood volume exceeding patient’s total blood volume within 24 hrs (or >10 units of PRBC). Acute complications: Metabolic: Hypocalcemia (citrate toxicity), hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia (from hemolysis), hypothermia, metabolic alkalosis. Coagulopathy: Due to dilution of platelets and clotting factors. Volume overload & ARDS. Prevention: Warm blood before transfusion, monitor electrolytes, give calcium gluconate if needed, replace platelets & FFP in balanced ratios. Key electrolyte changes in massive transfusion: Electrolyte Cause Change Calcium Citrate binding ↓ (Hypocalcemia) Potassium Leakage from stored RBCs ↑ (Hyperkalemia) Magnesium Citrate binding ↓ (Hypomagnesemia) Sodium Usually normal; slight ↑ if using older preservatives — Incorrect Options: Hypernatremia (Option A) – Not a major finding; sodium content in stored blood is minimal. Hyponatremia (Option B) – Not typically caused by transfusion. Hyperkalemia (Option D) – Possible in prolonged storage, but acute citrate-induced hypocalcemia is more characteristic in rapid large transfusions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A young female presents with ptosis showing diurnal variation. CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass identified as thymus gland cancer. Which receptor is affected in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A young female presents with ptosis showing diurnal variation. CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass identified as thymus gland cancer. Which receptor is affected in this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ

questions.solution: 51c8e471">autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, impairing neuromuscular transmission. Thymic abnormalities (hyperplasia or thymoma) are common in MG. In MG, antibody-mediated blockade and destruction of post-synaptic ACh receptors reduce the number of available receptors, leading to muscle weakness. Weakness worsens with activity and improves with rest (diurnal variation). The association with thymoma is due to aberrant immune activation in the thymus. Key features: Ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, proximal muscle weakness, preserved reflexes, and response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Myasthenia Gravis: Epidemiology: More common in young women and older men. Pathophysiology : Autoantibodies against post-synaptic nicotinic ACh receptors at NMJ → impaired depolarization of muscle fibers. Association: Thymic hyperplasia (65%) and thymoma (15%). Diagnosis: Edrophonium (Tensilon) test, anti-AChR antibody assay, repetitive nerve stimulation showing decremental response. Treatment: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine), immunosuppressants, thymectomy (if thymoma present), plasmapheresis/IVIG for crisis. NMJ disorders: Disorder Site of defect Antibody target / mechanism Myasthenia gravis Post-synaptic membrane Nicotinic ACh receptor Lambert–Eaton syndrome Presynaptic terminal Voltage-gated calcium channels Botulism Presynaptic terminal Inhibits ACh release (toxin action) Incorrect Options: Presynaptic ACh receptor (Option A) – No such pathology in MG; presynaptic issues are rare in autoimmune NMJ disease. Voltage-gated calcium channels at NMJ (Option C) – Targeted in Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, not MG. Acetylcholinesterase (Option D) – This enzyme breaks down ACh in synaptic cleft; it is inhibited pharmacologically in MG treatment, not attacked by antibodies. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia. He had developed diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. He was diagnosed as having GBS. What is the cause?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia. He had developed diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. He was diagnosed as having GBS. What is the cause?
questions.solution: p> Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy, most often triggered by infections like Campylobacter jejuni. It primarily affects myelinated large-diameter motor and sensory fibers (A and B fibers) , leading to weakness and areflexia. A- and B-fibers are myelinated nerve fibers responsible for motor function and some sensory modalities. In GBS, autoantibodies and immune cells attack the myelin sheath, impairing conduction. This demyelination disrupts both motor signals (causing weakness) and reflex arcs (causing areflexia). Guillain–Barré Syndrome: Trigger: Often post-infectious (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma). Pathophysiology: Autoimmune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves and nerve roots. Clinical features: Symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia, minimal sensory loss; may involve cranial nerves (bilateral facial palsy). Complications: Respiratory muscle involvement → respiratory failure; autonomic instability. Diagnosis: CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (↑ protein, normal cell count); NCS shows slowed conduction velocity. Treatment : IVIG or plasmapheresis; avoid steroids. Prognosis: Most recover fully, but some have residual deficits. Fiber types affected in GBS: Fiber Type Myelination Function A fibers Myelinated Motor + sensory B fibers Myelinated Preganglionic autonomic C fibers Unmyelinated Pain + temperature Incorrect Options: Demyelination of B-fibers (Option B) – B-fibers are affected, but not in isolation; A-fibers are also involved. Demyelination of the spinal cord (Option C) – GBS is a peripheral neuropathy, not a central spinal cord disorder. Cord inflammation (Option D) – Suggestive of myelitis, which presents with UMN signs and sensory level, not typical in GBS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A patient has developed a cough and weight loss for the last 3 months. Biopsy of lung mass shows expression of chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which paraneoplastic syndrome will most likely occur in this patient?
questions.solution: ndocrine tumor, such as small cell carcinoma of the lung. These tumors often produce ectopic ADH, leading to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). In SIADH, excessive ADH secretion causes water retention without corresponding sodium retention, resulting in dilutional hyponatremia and low plasma osmolality. Small cell lung carcinoma is notorious for secreting ectopic hormones, particularly ADH and ACTH. The presence of neuroendocrine markers confirms the tumor’s secretory nature. Small Cell Carcinoma: Origin: Neuroendocrine Kulchitsky cells in the lung. Markers: Chromogranin, synaptophysin, neuron-specific enolase (NSE). Paraneoplastic syndromes: SIADH (ADH), Cushing syndrome (ACTH), Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels). Histology: Small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, high mitotic count. Prognosis: Aggressive, early metastasis; often unresectable at diagnosis. Treatment: Combination chemotherapy ± radiotherapy; surgery rarely indicated. questions.stem: A patient presents with palpitations, headache, and sweating. His BP is 180/100 mmHg. 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with palpitations, headache, and sweating. His BP is 180/100 mmHg. 24-hour urinary metanephrine values are elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla. Classic symptoms are episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations with hypertension. Elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrines confirm catecholamine excess. Pheochromocytomas arise from chromaffin cells derived from neural crest tissue. Excess secretion of epinephrine and norepinephrine causes paroxysmal hypertension and sympathetic overactivity. Metanephrines are catecholamine metabolites, and their measurement in a 24-hour urine sample or plasma is the most sensitive test for diagnosis. Pheochromocytoma: Origin: Chromaffin cells (adrenal medulla). Rule of 10s: ~10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% in children. Associations: MEN 2A, MEN 2B, von Hippel–Lindau disease, NF1. Treatment: α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) before β-blockade, then surgical resection. Histology: Zellballen pattern (nests of cells with rich vascular stroma). Incorrect Options: Carcinoid tumor (Option A): Presents with flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm; diagnosis by urinary 5-HIAA, not metanephrines. Carcinoid crisis (Option C): Severe complication of carcinoid tumor with profound hypotension and bronchospasm; unrelated to catecholamines. Neuroblastoma (Option D): Pediatric tumor of adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain; elevated HVA/VMA (dopamine metabolites), not metanephrines in adults. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient with osteoarthritis, for the last 3 months, has been taking ibuprofen and has developed occult GI bleeding. Which is correct about the cause?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with osteoarthritis, for the last 3 months, has been taking ibuprofen and has developed occult GI bleeding. Which is correct about the cause?

options.label: A
options.text: PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced

options.label: C
options.text: PGE-1 and prostacyclin production were reduced

options.label: D
options.text: Mucosal injury due to inhibition of COX-2

questions.answerText: PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced
questions.solution: NSAIDs like ibuprofen inhibit COX enzymes, reducing prostaglandin (PGE₂) and prostacyclin synthesis. These mediators normally maintain gastric mucosal protection by increasing mucus and bicarbonate secretion and promoting mucosal blood flow. Loss of PGE₂ and prostacyclin leads to impaired gastric mucosal defense, making the mucosa susceptible to acid-induced injury and bleeding. This is the primary mechanism for NSAID-induced gastritis and peptic ulcers. COX-1 inhibition is particularly responsible for GI side effects, as it is involved in constitutive prostaglandin synthesis for mucosal protection. NSAID-induced GI injury: Mechanism: COX-1 inhibition → ↓ PGE₂, ↓ prostacyclin → ↓ mucus, ↓ bicarbonate, ↓ blood flow. Risk factors: High-dose/long-term NSAID use, elderly, alcohol, corticosteroids, H. pylori infection. Prevention: Co-prescription of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or misoprostol (PGE₁ analog). Histology: Superficial mucosal erosions with inflammatory infiltrates. Complications : Peptic ulcers, GI bleeding, perforation. Incorrect Options: Increased acid production (Option B): NSAIDs do not significantly increase gastric acid secretion; the main issue is reduced mucosal defense. PGE-1 and prostacyclin production reduced (Option C): The main gastric protective prostaglandin is PGE₂, not PGE₁. Mucosal injury due to inhibition of COX-2 (Option D): COX-2 inhibition is more linked to anti-inflammatory effects and cardiovascular risk, not primary GI mucosal damage (which is COX-1–mediated). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Explanation: The technical platform under India’s National Tele Mental Health Programme (NTMHP) designed specifically for delivering mental healthcare services through telephone, digital platforms, and online portals in a multi-tiered system is Tele-MANAS (Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States). Tele-MANAS: Launched by: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India. Objective: Provide accessible, affordable, and quality mental health services across India. Reduce stigma and bridge the treatment gap for mental illnesses. Structure: Tier 1: State Tele-MANAS cells with trained counsellors and mental health professionals answering calls via a toll-free helpline. questions.stem: Who is primarily responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning and maintaining their records under the national health system?
questions.stemHtml: Who is primarily responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning and maintaining their records under the national health system?
questions.solution: xplanation: Under India’s national health system, the Multipurpose Worker (Female), often synonymous with the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), is responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning and maintaining their records. This includes updating the Eligible Couple Register, tracking contraceptive use, and ensuring follow-up services. ASHAs and Anganwadi Workers assist in community mobilization and education but do not maintain the official eligible couple records. Multipurpose Worker (Female) / ANM in Family Planning: Role in Family Planning: Maintain Eligible Couple Register (ECR) at the sub-centre level. Identify eligible couples (married women aged 15–49 years). Record contraceptive choices and follow-up dates. Distribute contraceptives (condoms, OCPs) and counsel couples. questions.stem: A known case of hyperthyroidism, who is not on medication, is scheduled for total thyroidectomy. The PAC check was not done properly. What is the leading complication that can occur during surgery?
questions.stemHtml: A known case of hyperthyroidism, who is not on medication, is scheduled for total thyroidectomy. The PAC check was not done properly. What is the leading complication that can occur during surgery?
questions.solution: In uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, catecholamine sensitivity is increased, predisposing the patient to severe intraoperative arrhythmias, especially during surgical manipulation of the thyroid gland. A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism undergoing thyroidectomy is at high risk of thyroid storm, precipitated by surgical stress . This can manifest with tachyarrhythmias, hyperthermia, and hypertension. Arrhythmia (especially atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia) is the most immediate and dangerous intraoperative complication. Proper preoperative control with antithyroid drugs, β-blockers, and adequate preparation is essential. Incorrect Options: Hyperthermia (Option A): Can occur in thyroid storm but is not the leading intraoperative danger; arrhythmia is more acutely life-threatening. Hypothermia (Option B): Not typically associated with hyperthyroidism; more a concern in prolonged surgeries in cold OR environments. Hypothyroidism (Option D): Develops postoperatively, not during surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain of cluster headache. What is the best management?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old male presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain of cluster headache. What is the best management?
questions.solution: e acute abortive therapy for cluster headaches, rapidly relieving pain within 15–20 minutes in most cases. It is safe, well-tolerated, and works faster than most medications. Cluster headaches are severe unilateral headaches with autonomic features. Acute attacks require rapid-acting treatment — high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask or subcutaneous sumatriptan are first-line. Oxygen relieves pain by causing vasoconstriction and possibly modulating trigeminal-autonomic reflexes. Prophylaxis (e.g., verapamil, lithium) is started later to prevent recurrences, but during an acute attack, oxygen is the gold standard. questions.stem: Patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT scan shows a mass over the kidney with elevated ARR. What is the next best step for the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: Patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT scan shows a mass over the kidney with elevated ARR. What is the next best step for the management of this patient?
questions.solution: 9de85">hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome) due to an adrenal adenoma. In unilateral disease confirmed by imaging and biochemistry (elevated Aldosterone–Renin Ratio), surgical adrenalectomy is the treatment of choice. Hypertension + hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis + high ARR + adrenal mass suggests unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma. After confirming lateralization (often with adrenal venous sampling in some protocols), the definitive treatment is laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Medical management with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone/eplerenone) is reserved for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or non-surgical candidates. Primary Hyperaldosteronism: Feature Primary Hyperaldosteronism Common causes Adrenal adenoma (Conn’s), bilateral adrenal hyperplasia Key features Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis Screening Elevated ARR (Aldosterone–Renin Ratio) Confirmatory tests Saline suppression test, fludrocortisone suppression test Treatment – unilateral Surgical adrenalectomy Treatment – bilateral Spironolactone/eplerenone Incorrect Options: Spironolactone (Option A): First-line for bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical patients, not preferred for unilateral adenoma in a surgical candidate. ACTH stimulation test (Option C): Used for adrenal insufficiency diagnosis, not hyperaldosteronism. Dexamethasone suppression test (Option D): Used for diagnosing Cushing’s syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male has had chronic hypercalcemia for the last 1.5 years, but PTH levels are normal. Which of the following is most likely the cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male has had chronic hypercalcemia for the last 1.5 years, but PTH levels are normal. Which of the following is most likely the cause?
questions.solution: ss="customMeta" data-dictid="78912d4b7f16927771890c20495303">hypercalcemia but PTH is normal. This means the hypercalcemia is PTH-independent. Sarcoidosis, due to extra-renal production of calcitriol by activated macrophages, presents with hypercalcemia. Sarcoidosis: Multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology, characterized by non-caseating granulomas. In sarcoidosis, activated macrophages inside the granulomas express 1-α-hydroxylase, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D into 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). This leads to increased intestinal calcium absorption and persistent hypercalcemia. Because the calcium level is high, the parathyroid gland decreases PTH secretion, explaining the normal or low PTH levels in such cases. Feature Details Pathology Non-caseating granulomas in multiple organs Common Sites Lungs, lymph nodes, skin, eyes Lab Findings ↑ Serum ACE, ↑ calcium, normal/low PTH CXR Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy Diagnosis Clinical + radiological + biopsy confirmation Treatment Glucocorticoids for symptomatic disease Incorrect Options: Malignancy (Option A) – Can cause hypercalcemia via PTHrP or bone metastasis, but presentation is usually acute and associated with systemic symptoms like weight loss; chronic stable picture is less likely. Parathyroid hyperplasia (Option C) – Would cause elevated PTH, not normal PTH. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (Option D) – Causes hypocalcemia initially due to phosphate retention and decreased calcitriol synthesis; later may cause secondary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism with raised PTH, not normal. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A
options.text: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion

questions.solution: strong>tension pneumothorax – caused by air trapping in the pleural space under pressure. Key signs: Respiratory distress Hyperresonance (air in pleural space) Absent breath sounds (no lung expansion) Distended neck veins (↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return) Tracheal shift away from the affected side (mass effect) In tension pneumothorax, waiting for imaging can be fatal. Immediate needle decompression is done in the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line using a wide-bore cannula , followed by chest tube insertion. Tension Pneumothorax: Pathophysiology: Air enters the pleural space during inspiration but cannot exit (one-way valve mechanism). This increases intrapleural pressure → lung collapse → mediastinal shift → compression of heart and opposite lung → obstructive shock. Causes: trauma, mechanical ventilation, rib fractures, ruptured bleb. Emergency Management: Needle decompression (life-saving) – 2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line. Chest tube thoracostomy in the 4th/5th ICS mid-axillary line after decompression. Incorrect Options: Bedside CXR in casualty followed by chest tube insertion (Option A) – Wrong because waiting for imaging delays life-saving decompression. Pericardiocentesis (Option C) – For cardiac tamponade, not pneumothorax. Pleurodesis with doxycycline (Option D) – For recurrent pneumothorax, not for acute life-threatening tension pneumothorax. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A female presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is elevated. MRI shows pituitary adenoma. Best management for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A female presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is elevated. MRI shows pituitary adenoma. Best management for this patient?
questions.solution: g> The patient has hyperprolactinemia due to a pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). Hyperprolactinemia → suppresses GnRH → ↓ LH/FSH → menstrual irregularities and infertility. First-line treatment for prolactinomas is dopamine agonists (Bromocriptine or Cabergoline) as they inhibit prolactin secretion and can shrink the tumor. questions.stem: A child with progressive pallor and bone has an elevated HbS based on the HPLC report. Which is the best treatment to manage hemolysis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A child with progressive pallor and bone has an elevated HbS based on the HPLC report. Which is the best treatment to manage hemolysis in this patient?
questions.solution: /p> HPLC (High-Performance Liquid Chromatography) showing elevated HbS indicates Sickle Cell Disease (SCD). SCD is due to a mutation in β-globin gene → HbS polymerizes under low oxygen → sickling → chronic hemolysis + vaso-occlusive crises. Voxelotor is an HbS polymerization inhibitor that increases hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen, stabilizing the oxygenated form and reducing RBC sickling. This directly reduces hemolysis and improves anemia, making it the best treatment here for hemolysis control. Sickle Cell Disease (SCD): Pathophysiology: Point mutation (Glu → Val) in β-chain of Hb → polymerization in deoxygenated state → distorted RBCs → hemolysis + microvascular occlusion. Clinical features: Hemolytic anemia (pallor, jaundice, gallstones) Pain crises (bone pain, chest pain, abdomen) Dactylitis in children Splenic infarction → functional asplenia → infection risk Diagnosis: HPLC / electrophoresis (↑ HbS, ± HbF, ↓ HbA) Management: Hydroxyurea (↑ HbF, reduces crises) Voxelotor (↓ hemolysis, ↑ Hb) L-glutamine (↓ oxidative stress) Crizanlizumab (P-selectin inhibitor, ↓ vaso-occlusion) Supportive: vaccination, folate, transfusion if needed Incorrect Options: Hydroxyurea (Option A) – Increases HbF, reduces frequency of pain crises and acute chest syndrome, but has less direct effect on hemolysis than voxelotor. Azacytidine (Option B) – DNA methyltransferase inhibitor used in myelodysplastic syndromes/AML, not for SCD. Bortezomib (Option D) – Proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma, unrelated to SCD. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Voxelotor is an HbS polymerization inhibitor that increases hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen, stabilizing the oxygenated form and reducing RBC sickling. This directly reduces hemolysis and improves anemia, making it the best treatment here for hemolysis control.

Sickle Cell Disease (SCD):

  • Pathophysiology: Point mutation (Glu → Val) in β-chain of Hb → polymerization in deoxygenated state → distorted RBCs → hemolysis + microvascular occlusion.
  • Clinical features:
    • Hemolytic anemia (pallor, jaundice, gallstones)
    • Pain crises (bone pain, chest pain, abdomen)
    • Dactylitis in children
    • Splenic infarction → functional asplenia → infection risk
  • Diagnosis: HPLC / electrophoresis (↑ HbS, ± HbF, ↓ HbA)
  • Management:
    • Hydroxyurea (↑ HbF, reduces crises)
    • Voxelotor (↓ hemolysis, ↑ Hb)
    • L-glutamine (↓ oxidative stress)
    • Crizanlizumab (P-selectin inhibitor, ↓ vaso-occlusion)
    • Supportive: vaccination, folate, transfusion if needed

Incorrect Options:

Hydroxyurea (Option A) – Increases HbF, reduces frequency of pain crises and acute chest syndrome, but has less direct effect on hemolysis than voxelotor.

Azacytidine (Option B) – DNA methyltransferase inhibitor used in myelodysplastic syndromes/AML, not for SCD.

questions.stem: What is the probable diagnosis for a patient who exhibits miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil even in low light conditions?
questions.stemHtml: What is the probable diagnosis for a patient who exhibits miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil even in low light conditions?
questions.solution: miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil even in low light is suggestive of Horner syndrome. Ptosis is a result of the weakness of Müller muscle and miosis due to the unopposed action of the sphincter pupillae with resultant anisocoria. Pancoast tumor can compress the sympathetic nerves, leading to the classic triad of symptoms seen in Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis (constricted pupil), and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis (lack of sweating). Acquired Neurogenic Ptosis: Acquired ptosis with drooping of the upper eyelid caused by a disruption in the nerve supply to the muscles responsible for elevating the eyelid. Causes: Third Cranial (Oculomotor) Nerve Palsy: The third nerve can be damaged by trauma, ischemia, infection, tumor, or compression, causing ptosis and diplopia.Oculomotor nerve palsy causes ptosis as it supplies the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. The ptotic eyelid can be elevated with a frontalis sling or levator aponeurosis advancement. Horner's Syndrome: Involves a lesion in the sympathetic pathway , affecting the Müller’s muscle, leading to mild ptosis accompanied by miosis (pupil constriction) and anhidrosis (loss of sweating). Ophthalmoplegic migraine Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis: Topical apraclonidine test is now considered the test of choice. Apraclonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that also acts as a very weak alpha 1-adrenergic agonist; when topically applied in Horner’s syndrome, it causes dilation of the affected pupil and possibly lid elevation, without change to the normal pupil. Incorrect Options: Adie’s tonic people (Option A) It is a unilateral condition and is characterized by anisocoria (different size of pupil) and direct light reflex is sluggish or absent. Marcus gunn pupil (Option C) Aka relative afferent pupillary defect is characterized by paradoxical dilatation of both the pupil when light is flashed on the diseased eye. Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D) It is a specific sign of late-stage syphilis. The bilaterally small pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient with RTA is passing red color urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with RTA is passing red color urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.solution: >Myoglobinuria typically occurs after rhabdomyolysis , where muscle breakdown releases myoglobin and intracellular potassium into the bloodstream. Myoglobin is nephrotoxic, causing acute tubular necrosis (ATN) . Tubular injury in ATN often impairs potassium excretion, resulting in Type 4 RTA physiology , which is characterized by hyperkalemia and mild metabolic acidosis. The potassium rise is further exacerbated by direct release from damaged muscle cells. Incorrect Options: Hypernatremia (Option A): Less common in ATN; if anything, sodium tends to be low due to renal losses and fluid shifts. Hyponatremia (Option C): Can occur in kidney injury but not a hallmark feature of RTA with rhabdomyolysis. Hypokalemia (Option D): Seen in Type 1 (distal) and Type 2 (proximal) RTA, but not in Type 4 RTA or ATN — here potassium retention predominates. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient after RTA had a renal shut down. Work-up shows: FeNa: < 1%, Urine osmolality: 300 mOsm/kg, Urinary sodium: 40 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient after RTA had a renal shut down. Work-up shows: FeNa: &lt; 1%, Urine osmolality: 300 mOsm/kg, Urinary sodium: 40 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: strong> Explanation: This presentation points to intrinsic renal injury , specifically ATN , where damaged renal tubules lose the ability to reabsorb sodium and concentrate urine. Key features in this case: Urinary sodium > 40 mEq/L → tubular sodium wasting Urine osmolality ~300 mOsm/kg → isosthenuria (urine similar to plasma) FeNa < 1% is more typical of pre-renal AKI, but in early ATN or mixed states it can also be low. Here, the high urinary sodium and poor urine concentration outweigh FeNa alone, supporting ATN. Clinical Phases of ATN Phase Description Prerenal Phase (Pre-ATN) ↓ Renal perfusion (e.g., hypovolemia, CHF) Tubular function intact FeNa <1%, BUN:Cr >20 Responds to fluids Reversible if corrected early Initiation Phase Time of original injury (ischemia/toxins) Mild ↓ GFR, slight ↑ creatinine Urine output may be normal Damage beginning but potentially reversible Extension Phase Ongoing injury + inflammation (days 1–3) Tubular necrosis, obstruction Key sign: ↑ Creatinine + new oliguria despite fluids FeNa >2%, granular casts may appear Maintenance Phase Established tubular damage Low GFR, sustained ↑ creatinine/BUN Oliguric or non-oliguric Electrolyte imbalances: hyperkalemia, acidosis Recovery (Repair) Phase Tubular regeneration Polyuric phase: ↑ urine output Gradual ↓ creatinine Risk: volume depletion, electrolyte loss Incorrect Options: Pre-renal AKI (Option B): Characterized by low urinary sodium (<20 mEq/L) and high urine osmolality (>500 mOsm/kg) . Post-renal AKI (Option C): Labs are variable; diagnosis usually requires imaging evidence of obstruction. Renal AKI (Option D): Too broad; ATN is the specific intrinsic renal diagnosis here. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>

Explanation:

  • This presentation points to intrinsic renal injury, specifically ATN, where damaged renal tubules lose the ability to reabsorb sodium and concentrate urine.
  • Key features in this case:
    • Urinary sodium > 40 mEq/L → tubular sodium wasting
    • Urine osmolality ~300 mOsm/kg → isosthenuria (urine similar to plasma)
    • FeNa < 1% is more typical of pre-renal AKI, but in early ATN or mixed states it can also be low.
    • Here, the high urinary sodium and poor urine concentration outweigh FeNa alone, supporting ATN.

Clinical Phases of ATN

Phase

Description

Prerenal Phase (Pre-ATN)
  • ↓ Renal perfusion (e.g., hypovolemia, CHF)
  • Tubular function intact
  • FeNa <1%, BUN:Cr >20
  • Responds to fluids
  • Reversible if corrected early

Initiation Phase
  • Time of original injury (ischemia/toxins)
  • Mild ↓ GFR, slight ↑ creatinine
  • Urine output may be normal
  • Damage beginning but potentially reversible

Extension Phase

  • Ongoing injury + inflammation (days 1–3)
  • Tubular necrosis, obstruction
  • Key sign: ↑ Creatinine + new oliguria despite fluids
  • FeNa >2%, granular casts may appear

Maintenance Phase
  • Established tubular damage
  • Low GFR, sustained ↑ creatinine/BUN
  • Oliguric or non-oliguric
  • Electrolyte imbalances: hyperkalemia, acidosis

Recovery (Repair) Phase
  • Tubular regeneration
  • Polyuric phase: ↑ urine output
  • Gradual ↓ creatinine
  • Risk: volume depletion, electrolyte loss

 

Incorrect Options:

Pre-renal AKI (Option B):

  • Characterized by low urinary sodium (<20 mEq/L) and high urine osmolality (>500 mOsm/kg).

Post-renal AKI (Option C):

  • Labs are variable; diagnosis usually requires imaging evidence of obstruction.

Renal AKI (Option D):

  • Too broad; ATN is the specific intrinsic renal diagnosis here.

questions.stem: A patient is in ICU and there is a failed attempt of subclavian catheterization. Shortly after, BP drops and the pulse rises. What is the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient is in ICU and there is a failed attempt of subclavian catheterization. Shortly after, BP drops and the pulse rises. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: > Subclavian vein catheterization carries a significant risk of pleural injury , which can cause pneumothorax . Air entry into the pleural space leads to reduced venous return , causing hypotension and reflex tachycardia. In the ICU setting, this can rapidly progress to tension pneumothorax , which is life-threatening and requires urgent decompression. Typical signs: sudden drop in BP, tachycardia, respiratory distress, unilateral decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance on percussion. Incorrect Options: Displacement of ET (Option B): Would cause hypoxia and respiratory distress, but is not directly related to subclavian line attempt. Air embolism (Option C): Can occur during line placement, but presents with sudden cardiovascular collapse and possibly a "mill wheel" murmur; pneumothorax is more common post failed subclavian attempt. Dislodgement of ET (Option D): Would cause airway compromise but unrelated to catheterization unless ET manipulation occurred. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient had a road traffic accident (RTA). NCCT head was normal on admission. The patient later died after several days in the ICU due to coma. Brain biopsy revealed multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient had a road traffic accident (RTA). NCCT head was normal on admission. The patient later died after several days in the ICU due to coma. Brain biopsy revealed multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: > Explanation: Diffuse axonal injury is a primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma (e.g., RTA). These forces disrupt axons in the white matter , corpus callosum, and brainstem. On initial imaging, NCCT may be normal or show only tiny petechial hemorrhages ; the condition is often diagnosed clinically or via MRI . Histopathology (or biopsy) reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages in deep white matter tracts. DAI often leads to immediate or prolonged coma without a lucid interval and carries a high mortality rate. Incorrect Options: Ischemic injury (Option A): Usually presents with territorial infarcts and hypoxic changes, not punctate hemorrhages in white matter. Intraventricular bleeding (Option C): Would be evident on CT and localized to ventricular system, not diffuse white matter punctate hemorrhages. Subdural hemorrhage (Option D): Characterized by crescent-shaped collection on CT, caused by tearing of bridging veins — not microscopic hemorrhages. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>

Explanation:

  • These forces disrupt axons in the white matter, corpus callosum, and brainstem.
  • On initial imaging, NCCT may be normal or show only tiny petechial hemorrhages; the condition is often diagnosed clinically or via MRI.
  • Histopathology (or biopsy) reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages in deep white matter tracts.
  • DAI often leads to immediate or prolonged coma without a lucid interval and carries a high mortality rate.

 

Incorrect Options:

Ischemic injury (Option A): Usually presents with territorial infarcts and hypoxic changes, not punctate hemorrhages in white matter.

Intraventricular bleeding (Option C): Would be evident on CT and localized to ventricular system, not diffuse white matter punctate hemorrhages.

Subdural hemorrhage (Option D): Characterized by crescent-shaped collection on CT, caused by tearing of bridging veins — not microscopic hemorrhages.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with fever and altered sensorium. Peripheral smear shows multiple ring stages. Best treatment is?
questions.solution: i>Fever with altered sensorium in malaria indicates cerebral malaria — a severe form most often due to Plasmodium falciparum . Multiple ring forms on smear strongly suggest falciparum malaria. Artesunate is preferred over quinine for severe malaria as per WHO guidelines, given its better safety profile, faster parasite clearance, and lower mortality. It is administered intravenously in the acute setting. Incorrect Options: Primaquine (Option A): Used for radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale to target hypnozoites in the liver, not for acute severe falciparum malaria. Quinine (Option B): Historically the drug of choice for severe falciparum malaria, but now replaced by IV artesunate due to superior efficacy and safety. Chloroquine (Option C) : Effective for chloroquine-sensitive malaria, but most P. falciparum strains are resistant, making it inappropriate in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What defect is seen in Bernard Soulier syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: What defect is seen in Bernard Soulier syndrome?
questions.solution: i>Bernard–Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive platelet disorder characterized by a defect in platelet adhesion due to deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) complex, which is the receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF). This defect prevents platelets from binding to exposed subendothelial vWF during vascular injury, leading to defective primary hemostasis. Clinically, it presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, and thrombocytopenia with giant platelets on peripheral smear. Incorrect Options: Deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa receptor (Option A): Seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia — causes defective platelet aggregation, not adhesion. Deficiency of von Willebrand factor (Option C): Seen in von Willebrand disease — results in both defective platelet adhesion and secondary coagulation defect due to reduced factor VIII stability. Deficiency of ADP receptors (Option D): Seen in rare platelet function disorders like P2Y12 receptor defects — affects aggregation via ADP pathway, not adhesion. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: n: Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize recipient tissues as foreign and mount an immune response. This typically happens in immunocompromised recipients who are unable to reject the donor T cells. In the context of a skin graft (especially from another immunocompromised individual where donor lymphocytes may survive), GVHD can cause systemic symptoms (fever, rash, liver dysfunction, diarrhea) along with local changes like skin contractures. Incorrect Options: Graft failure (Option B): Results from the inability of the graft to establish blood supply, leading to necrosis — it occurs early, not weeks later, and does not cause systemic immune symptoms. Rejection due to recipient T8 cells (Option C): This is host-versus-graft rejection, not GVHD, and requires an immunocompetent recipient — which is not the case here. Delayed wound healing (Option D): Common in immunocompromised states but does not explain systemic features or the contractures caused by immune-mediated damage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with complaints of eye strain. The given image shows the focus of light rays in different meridians in the eye. Which refractive error is present in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with complaints of eye strain. The given image shows the focus of light rays in different meridians in the eye. Which refractive error is present in this patient?
questions.solution: ge of Sturm’s conoid demonstrates that parallel light rays do not converge to a single focal point, but rather form two focal lines at different distances due to unequal refractive power in different meridians of the cornea or lens. This optical phenomenon is characteristic of astigmatism , where light rays along one meridian focus in front of the retina while rays along the perpendicular meridian focus either behind or at a different point. Astigmatism causes blurred or distorted vision and eye strain (asthenopia), especially with prolonged near tasks. Sturm’s conoid in Astigmatism: Light rays from an object pass through two principal meridians with different curvatures. Each meridian has its own focal length → creates two focal lines (not a single point). The area between these two focal lines is called the Sturm’s conoid. The best vision is achieved at the circle of least confusion , located between the two focal lines. Incorrect Options: Amblyopia (Option A): Reduced vision in one or both eyes due to abnormal visual development in childhood; unrelated to optical focusing errors like those shown in Sturm’s conoid. Hypermetropia (Option B): Farsightedness due to the eye being too short or the cornea too flat, causing light to focus behind the retina; it produces a single focal point (not two) and does not show Sturm’s conoid. Presbyopia (Option D): Age-related loss of accommodation due to decreased lens elasticity; affects near vision but does not produce two focal lines in different meridians. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A myopic patient presents with complaints of flashes and floaters. On examination, a deep anterior chamber is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A myopic patient presents with complaints of flashes and floaters. On examination, a deep anterior chamber is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ic patient with flashes (photopsia) , floaters , and a deep anterior chamber suggests posterior vitreous detachment with retinal tear. This allows liquefied vitreous to pass into the subretinal space, leading to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment . Key mechanism: Myopia → long axial length → retinal thinning + lattice degeneration → predisposes to retinal breaks. These breaks allow fluid entry under retina → separation from retinal pigment epithelium. Deep anterior chamber in this context is due to elongation of the globe and posterior shift of the lens–iris diaphragm in high myopia. Type of Retinal Detachment Clinical Features Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment 1. Floaters (dark spots) due to rapid vitreous degeneration. 2. Photopsia (flashes of light) caused by retinal irritation from vitreous movements. 3. Gradual visual field loss, initially localized, progressing to total vision loss as detachment spreads. 4. Dark veil/cloud in front of the eye , particularly when detachment reaches the posterior region. 5. Sudden, painless vision loss in large, central detachment. 6. Retinal breaks may be round, horseshoe-shaped, slit-like, or large anterior dialysis. 7. Vitreous pigments (tobacco dusting or Shaffer sign ) are seen in the anterior vitreous with posterior vitreous detachment. 8. Old retinal detachment shows retinal thinning, subretinal demarcation lines (high water marks), and secondary intraretinal cysts. Tractional Retinal Detachment (Option C ruled out) 1. Gradual, progressive visual loss 2. Typically painless 3. No associated flashes or floaters 4. Vitreoretinal bands present 5. No retinal breaks 6. Detached area - concave and localized 7. No shifting fluid Exudative Retinal Detachment (Option A ruled out) 1. Painless and sudden or gradual visual loss 2. No photopsia, holes/ tears, folds and undulations. 3. Smooth and convex with pigmentary disturbances 4. Rounded and fixed with neovascularization on the tumor summit. 5. Shifting fluid - changing the position of the detached area with gravity - hallmark feature. Central serous retinopathy (Option D): Localized serous detachment of the neurosensory retina at the macula, seen in young stressed males; presents with central vision blurring and metamorphopsia, not flashes/floaters. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Deep anterior chamber in this context is due to elongation of the globe and posterior shift of the lens–iris diaphragm in high myopia.

    • Type of Retinal Detachment

    Clinical Features

    Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment

    1. Floaters (dark spots) due to rapid vitreous degeneration.

    2. Photopsia (flashes of light) caused by retinal irritation from vitreous movements.

    3. Gradual visual field loss, initially localized, progressing to total vision loss as detachment spreads.

    4. Dark veil/cloud in front of the eye, particularly when detachment reaches the posterior region.

    5. Sudden, painless vision loss in large, central detachment.

    6. Retinal breaks may be round, horseshoe-shaped, slit-like, or large anterior dialysis.

    7. Vitreous pigments (tobacco dusting or Shaffer sign) are seen in the anterior vitreous with posterior vitreous detachment.

    8. Old retinal detachment shows retinal thinning, subretinal demarcation lines (high water marks), and secondary intraretinal cysts.

    Tractional Retinal Detachment (Option C ruled out)

    1. Gradual, progressive visual loss

    2. Typically painless

    3. No associated flashes or floaters

    4. Vitreoretinal bands present

    5. No retinal breaks

    6. Detached area - concave and localized

    1. Painless and sudden or gradual visual loss

    2. No photopsia, holes/ tears, folds and undulations.

    3. Smooth and convex with pigmentary disturbances

    4. Rounded and fixed with neovascularization on the tumor summit.

    5. Shifting fluid - changing the position of the detached area with gravity - hallmark feature.

questions.solution: Explanation: The presence of ocular pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze can be seen in both acute uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma , but here the combination of inflammation signs (ciliary congestion, corneal edema) and pupil changes points toward acute uveitis as the answer given. In uveitis, cells and flare in anterior chamber cause corneal haze, and pupil is irregular or sluggishly reactive due to posterior synechiae; early on it may appear mid-dilated. The shallow anterior chamber here may be due to ciliary body swelling pushing the iris forward in acute inflammation. Key features of Acute Uveitis: Pain, photophobia, redness (ciliary flush). Decreased vision due to corneal edema and aqueous flare. Irregular or sluggish pupil (posterior synechiae). May cause shallow anterior chamber due to ciliary body congestion. Anterior Uveitis Definition : Most common type of uveitis affecting the anterior segment of the eye. Clinical Features : Pain Redness Photophobia (sensitivity to light) Blepharospasm (involuntary blinking) Serous discharge Blurring and diminished vision Examination Findings : Keratic Precipitates (KPs) : Non-Granulomatous : Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes Granulomatous : Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs"; composed of macrophages Location : Typically found in the lower cornea due to convection currents in aqueous humor; this area is known as Arlt's triangle Aqueous Cells : Indicator of active inflammation Aqueous Flare : Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues Muddy Iris : Edema in the iris caused by protein leakage Miosis : Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue Nodules on the Iris : Koeppe's Nodules : At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis Busacca Nodules : At the b ase of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis Complications : (Findings) Posterior Synechiae : Iris adheres to the lens; may lead to festooned-shaped pupil Secclusio Pupil/Ring Synechiae : Adhesion along the entire pupillary border; can lead to Iris Bombe and peripheral anterior synechiae, causing angle closure glaucoma Occlusio Pupil : Covers the whole surface of the lens Cyclitic Membrane Rubeosis Iridis : New vessel formation on the iris Incorrect Options: Acute conjunctivitis (Option B): Presents with diffuse redness, mucopurulent or watery discharge; vision usually normal, cornea clear, pupil reactive, anterior chamber normal depth. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option C): Sudden severe pain, markedly decreased vision, halos around lights, very high IOP , fixed mid-dilated pupil, shallow anterior chamber - however, it is typically more painful, with headache/nausea, and the hallmark is IOP >40 mmHg with rock-hard globe. Central retinal artery occlusion (Option D): Sudden painless monocular vision loss; examination shows pale retina with cherry-red spot, no corneal haze, no anterior chamber shallowing. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of ocular pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze can be seen in both acute uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma, but here the combination of inflammation signs (ciliary congestion, corneal edema) and pupil changes points toward acute uveitis as the answer given.
  • In uveitis, cells and flare in anterior chamber cause corneal haze, and pupil is irregular or sluggishly reactive due to posterior synechiae; early on it may appear mid-dilated.
  • The shallow anterior chamber here may be due to ciliary body swelling pushing the iris forward in acute inflammation.

Key features of Acute Uveitis:

  1. Pain, photophobia, redness (ciliary flush).
  2. Decreased vision due to corneal edema and aqueous flare.
  3. Irregular or sluggish pupil (posterior synechiae).
  4. May cause shallow anterior chamber due to ciliary body congestion.

Anterior Uveitis

Definition: Most common type of uveitis affecting the anterior segment of the eye.

Clinical Features:

  • Pain
  • Redness
  • Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
  • Blepharospasm (involuntary blinking)
  • Serous discharge
  • Blurring and diminished vision

Examination Findings:

  • Keratic Precipitates (KPs):
    • Non-Granulomatous: Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes
    • Granulomatous: Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs"; composed of macrophages
    • Location: Typically found in the lower cornea due to convection currents in aqueous humor; this area is known as Arlt's triangle

  • Aqueous Cells:
    • Indicator of active inflammation
  • Aqueous Flare:
    • Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues
  • Muddy Iris:
    • Edema in the iris caused by protein leakage
  • Miosis:
    • Constricted pupil due to toxins released from inflamed tissue
  • Nodules on the Iris:
    • Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis
    • Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis

Complications: (Findings)

  • Posterior Synechiae: Iris adheres to the lens; may lead to festooned-shaped pupil

  • Secclusio Pupil/Ring Synechiae: Adhesion along the entire pupillary border; can lead to Iris Bombe and peripheral anterior synechiae, causing angle closure glaucoma
  • Occlusio Pupil: Covers the whole surface of the lens
  • Cyclitic Membrane
  • Rubeosis Iridis: New vessel formation on the iris

Incorrect Options:

  • Acute conjunctivitis (Option B): Presents with diffuse redness, mucopurulent or watery discharge; vision usually normal, cornea clear, pupil reactive, anterior chamber normal depth.
  • Acute congestive glaucoma (Option C): Sudden severe pain, markedly decreased vision, halos around lights, very high IOP, fixed mid-dilated pupil, shallow anterior chamber - however, it is typically more painful, with headache/nausea, and the hallmark is IOP >40 mmHg with rock-hard globe.
  • Central retinal artery occlusion (Option D): Sudden painless monocular vision loss; examination shows pale retina with cherry-red spot, no corneal haze, no anterior chamber shallowing.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a painless ulcer in the eye. On examination, a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium is seen on the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with a painless ulcer in the eye. On examination, a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium is seen on the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Explanation: A painless corneal ulcer indicates reduced or absent corneal sensation. The finding of a long, branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium but without the typical raised edges and terminal bulbs of herpes simplex keratitis suggests a neurotrophic ulcer . Neurotrophic keratopathy results from damage to trigeminal nerve sensory supply, leading to impaired healing and epithelial breakdown, producing branching epithelial defects. Neurotrophic Ulcer: Painless despite corneal epithelial defect. Decreased corneal sensation and epithelial desquamation. Often branching/irregular ulcer margins. Causes: herpes simplex/zoster, trigeminal nerve damage (tumor, surgery), diabetes, chronic topical medication toxicity. May follow procedures like Gasserian ganglion removal or blockage, often used in treating trigeminal neuralgia. Poor healing tendency due to loss of corneal reflex and trophic support. Incorrect Options: Fungal ulcer (Option A): Usually follows trauma with vegetative matter; presents with pain, feathery margins, satellite lesions, and hypopyon; not typically painless and branching like in neurotrophic ulcer. Dendritic ulcer (Option B): Caused by herpes simplex virus; branching ulcer with terminal bulbs that stain with fluorescein; usually painful (unless corneal sensation is already lost). Bacterial corneal ulcer (Option C): Acute, painful, purulent ulcer with stromal infiltration and hypopyon; rapid progression; not painless and not typically branching. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with eye examination findings of a deep anterior chamber and jet-black pupil is prescribed +12D glasses. Likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old patient with eye examination findings of a deep anterior chamber and jet-black pupil is prescribed +12D glasses. Likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: strong> Deep anterior chamber → suggests absence of crystalline lens. Jet-black pupil → no lens reflections seen. +12D prescription → large convex lens to replace lost refractive power of natural lens. Aphakia = complete absence of the natural lens (usually post-cataract surgery without IOL implantation). Without the lens, refractive power decreases drastically (~+15D needed), so strong convex lenses are prescribed. Causes: Post-cataract extraction without IOL, trauma, congenital. Features: Deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis, jet-black pupil, high hypermetropia (+10 to +15D). Aphakia: Definition Absence of crystalline lens from the eye. Aetiology Congenital absence (rare) Surgical removal (common) Traumatic extrusion of lens (rare) Posterior lens dislocation (optical aphakia) Optical Effects High hypermetropia Reduced eye power to +44 D (from +60 D) Symptoms Defective vision (far and near) Erythropsia and cyanopsia (abnormal red and blue color defect) Signs Limbal/corneal scar (in surgical cases) Deep anterior chamber Iridodonesis & Jet-black pupil Only 2 Purkinje images (normal: 4) Hypermetropic small optic disc Treatment Correct refractive error with: Spectacles: the problem of spherical aberration and roving ring scotoma (jack-in-the-box phenomenon) Contact lenses Intraocular lenses (IOL) - best method Refractive LASIK surgery Incorrect Options: Pseudophakia (Option A): Eye has an artificial intraocular lens post-cataract surgery; patient usually needs minimal refractive correction (not +12D). Myopia (Option C): Nearsightedness; requires concave (minus) lenses; opposite of the strong convex lenses seen here. Hypermetropia (Option D): Farsightedness; needs convex lenses, but typically much lower power (+1D to +4D), not as high as +12D. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>
  • Deep anterior chamber → suggests absence of crystalline lens.
  • Jet-black pupil → no lens reflections seen.
  • +12D prescription → large convex lens to replace lost refractive power of natural lens.
  • Aphakia = complete absence of the natural lens (usually post-cataract surgery without IOL implantation).
  • Without the lens, refractive power decreases drastically (~+15D needed), so strong convex lenses are prescribed.
  • Causes: Post-cataract extraction without IOL, trauma, congenital.
  • Features: Deep anterior chamber, iridodonesis, jet-black pupil, high hypermetropia (+10 to +15D).

    • Aphakia:

    Definition
    • Absence of crystalline lens from the eye.

    Aetiology
    • Congenital absence (rare)
    • Surgical removal (common)
    • Traumatic extrusion of lens (rare)
    • Posterior lens dislocation (optical aphakia)

    Optical Effects
    • High hypermetropia
    • Reduced eye power to +44 D (from +60 D)

    Symptoms
    • Defective vision (far and near)
    • Erythropsia and cyanopsia (abnormal red and blue color defect)

    Signs
    • Limbal/corneal scar (in surgical cases)
    • Deep anterior chamber
    • Iridodonesis & Jet-black pupil
    • Only 2 Purkinje images (normal: 4)
    • Hypermetropic small optic disc

    Treatment

    Correct refractive error with:

    • Spectacles: the problem of spherical aberration and roving ring scotoma (jack-in-the-box phenomenon)
    • Contact lenses
    • Intraocular lenses (IOL) - best method
    • Refractive LASIK surgery

    Incorrect Options:

    • Pseudophakia (Option A): Eye has an artificial intraocular lens post-cataract surgery; patient usually needs minimal refractive correction (not +12D).
    • Myopia (Option C): Nearsightedness; requires concave (minus) lenses; opposite of the strong convex lenses seen here.
    • Hypermetropia (Option D): Farsightedness; needs convex lenses, but typically much lower power (+1D to +4D), not as high as +12D.

questions.stem: A man presents to the hospital with a bizarre behavior. He is unable to recall his personal identity and has no memory of how he traveled 100 km to reach the hospital. A collateral history reveals he experienced a traumatic earthquake a few months ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A man presents to the hospital with a bizarre behavior. He is unable to recall his personal identity and has no memory of how he traveled 100 km to reach the hospital. A collateral history reveals he experienced a traumatic earthquake a few months ago. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Explanation: The patient's presentation is a classic example of a dissociative disorder, specifically dissociative amnesia with a dissociative fugue. The key features that point to this diagnosis are: Inability to Recall Personal Information: The patient is unable to remember his personal identity and significant past events. This memory loss is not due to a medical condition. Following a Traumatic Event: The amnesia is directly linked to a recent, severe traumatic stressor (the earthquake). This is a hallmark of dissociative disorders. Dissociative Fugue: The patient's purposeful travel over a long distance (100 km) without any memory of the journey is characteristic of a dissociative fugue, a subtype of dissociative amnesia. Incorrect Options: Dissociative identity disorder (Option B) involves the presence of two or more distinct personality states (or "alters"), which is not described in this case. Schizophrenia (Option C) is a psychotic disorder characterized by symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thought, none of which are mentioned in the patient's presentation. Global amnesia (Option D) is a broad term that can be caused by organic, non-psychiatric conditions such as stroke or head injury. Since the patient's amnesia is clearly linked to a traumatic event and not an organic cause, dissociative amnesia is the more specific and likely diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old software engineer presents with sleep disturbances, low mood, and stress for the past 3 months. He attributes his symptoms to ongoing problems at work. He has no prior psychiatric history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old software engineer presents with sleep disturbances, low mood, and stress for the past 3 months. He attributes his symptoms to ongoing problems at work. He has no prior psychiatric history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: strong>Explanation: The patient's symptoms are a classic presentation of adjustment disorder. The diagnostic criteria for this condition are: Emotional or Behavioral Symptoms: The patient exhibits emotional or behavioral symptoms (sleep disturbances, low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor. Timeline: The symptoms must begin within three months of the onset of the stressor (in this case, excessive work pressure). Marked Distress and Impairment: The symptoms cause marked distress that is disproportionate to the severity of the stressor and lead to significant impairment in social or occupational functioning (difficulty maintaining work-life balance). Exclusion of Other Disorders: The symptoms do not meet the criteria for another specific mental disorder, such as major depressive disorder or a psychotic disorder. Incorrect Options: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) (Option B) is a more chronic condition, requiring at least six months of excessive worry and anxiety about multiple events or activities. The patient's symptoms are directly tied to a specific, recent stressor. Acute stress disorder (Option C) is a response to a traumatic event (e.g., a natural disaster, assault, or serious accident) and its symptoms last for a shorter duration (from three days to one month). The patient's symptoms are from work pressure, which is a significant stressor but not a traumatic event. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Option D) also requires exposure to a traumatic event and includes symptoms of re-experiencing the event, avoidance of related stimuli, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal. This is not consistent with the patient's presentation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with painful lid swelling. On examination, a pus point is observed at the base of an eyelash. Which of the following glands is involved?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with painful lid swelling. On examination, a pus point is observed at the base of an eyelash. Which of the following glands is involved?
questions.solution: 6e0c472d4a">swelling with a visible opus point (localized yellowish spot of pus) at the base of an eyelash is characteristic of external hordeolum (stye) . An external hordeolum is an acute bacterial infection (usually Staphylococcus aureus ) of the sebaceous glands of Zeis located at the eyelash follicle. The pain is due to acute inflammation, and the pus may discharge spontaneously, relieving symptoms. Condition Definition & Features Treatment External Hordeolum (Stye) Acute suppurative inflammation of a lash follicle and associated glands of Zeis or Moll. Most common causative organism - Staphylococcus aureus. Symptoms: Acute pain with swelling on the anterior lid margin, watering and photophobia. Hot compresses 2-3 times daily. Evacuate pus by epilating involved cilia when pus point forms. Rarely, surgical incision for large abscess. Antibiotic eye drops and ointment. Systemic anti-inflammatory and analgesics. Systemic antibiotics for early infection control. Identify and treat predisposing conditions in recurrent cases. Incorrect Options: Meibomian gland (Option B): Sebaceous glands in the tarsal plate; acute infection → internal hordeolum (pus points to conjunctival side), chronic blockage → chalazion; not at eyelash base. Lacrimal gland (Option C): Located in the superolateral orbit; inflammation (dacryoadenitis) causes painful swelling in outer upper eyelid — not localized to eyelash follicle. Moll gland (Option D): Modified sweat glands at eyelash follicles; infection causes less common external hordeolum (Moll type) , but opus point at eyelash base is more classically due to Zeis gland infection. @Neet_pg_bot
