VIP (Option C) – Elevated in VIPoma; causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome), and no duodenal nodules with GERD. Glucagon (Option D) – Elevated in glucagonoma; presents with necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, and anemia, typically in the pancreas, not the duodenum. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 7-year-old male child was brought to the EMR 6 hours after a burn and was having 22% BSA burns. On examination, cool extremities, BP - 92/50mmHg, PR - 56 BPM. Urine output since burn episode: 30ml. What is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old male child was brought to the EMR 6 hours after a burn and was having 22% BSA burns. On examination, cool extremities, BP - 92/50mmHg, PR - 56 BPM. Urine output since burn episode: 30ml. What is the next step in management?
questions.solution: he child has burn shock — evidenced by hypotension, bradycardia (late sign in children), cool extremities, and low urine output. In pediatric burns, >15% BSA requires urgent IV fluid resuscitation to prevent progression to multi-organ failure. This patient is 6 hours post-burn, meaning there is already an ongoing deficit that must be corrected promptly. Therefore, an initial bolus: 10 ml/kg of Ringer’s lactate is recommended to restore circulation before calculated maintenance fluids. Colloids are not given early because, during the first 24 hours, capillary permeability is markedly increased → colloids leak into the interstitium → worsen edema. Colloids (e.g., albumin) are generally started after 24 hours. options.label: D

questions.solution: mMeta" data-dictid="83e66fab2f1692777190a43a6e300f">intubation and ventilation are not possible is known as a “cannot intubate, cannot ventilate” (CICV) scenario → this is a surgical airway emergency. Severe maxillofacial trauma often distorts airway anatomy, making both oral and nasal intubation impossible. In CICV, the fastest and most accessible surgical airway is emergency cricothyrotomy. Although tracheostomy provides a definitive airway, it takes longer and requires a more stable patient; not suitable for immediate life-threatening hypoxia. Cricothyrotomy allows rapid oxygenation within 30–60 seconds. Cricothyrotomy: Indications: CICV situations Severe facial trauma Upper airway obstruction Massive facial burns/swelling Landmarks: Thyroid cartilage Cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid & cricoid cartilage) Procedure: Palpate the cricothyroid membrane. Make a vertical skin incision, a horizontal membrane incision. Insert a tracheostomy or endotracheal tube. Advantages: Quick, minimal equipment, bypasses upper airway obstruction. Limitations: Should be converted to tracheostomy within 24–72 hrs to prevent subglottic stenosis. questions.stem: A 13-year-old male was brought to OPD with pain right side testes after being hit by a cricket ball 2 hours back. On examination, severe testicular pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the next step?
questions.stemHtml: A 13-year-old male was brought to OPD with pain right side testes after being hit by a cricket ball 2 hours back. On examination, severe testicular pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. What is the next step?
questions.solution: ith testicular pain and absent cremasteric reflex is suggestive of testicular torsion. Guidelines recommend color Doppler ultrasound as the first investigation to check testicular blood flow. USG Arterial Doppler will show: Absent or reduced arterial flow → confirms torsion → immediate surgical exploration. Normal or increased flow → rules out torsion, suggests inflammation. However, if clinical suspicion is extremely high (classic torsion features), exploration is preferred without delay. Testicular Torsion: Twisting of the spermatic cord → cuts off arterial supply to the testis → surgical emergency. Peak age: Neonates and adolescents (12–18 years). Causes: Bell-clapper deformity, trauma, sudden movements, or spontaneous. Key clinical signs: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain High-riding, horizontally oriented testis Absent cremasteric reflex Negative Prehn’s sign (no relief on elevation) Golden period: Salvage rate is best if detorsion is done within 6 hours; irreversible damage after ~12 hours. Treatment: Surgical exploration, detorsion, and bilateral orchidopexy (fixation of both testes). On examination, he has darkly pigmented spots on his lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy presents with multiple episodes of abdominal pain and a history of passing blood in his stools. On examination, he has darkly pigmented spots on his lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: this classic triad is diagnostic of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (PJS) , a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by STK11/LKB1 gene mutation. There is an increased risk for multiple cancers: GI (colon, stomach, pancreas), breast, ovary, cervix, and testes. Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome (PJS): Inheritance: Autosomal dominant. Gene: STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene mutation (chromosome 19p13.3). Pathology: Multiple hamartomatous polyps (non-neoplastic, but with malignant potential due to genetic instability). Features: Mucocutaneous pigmentation → dark spots on lips, buccal mucosa, fingertips. Pigmentation is due to melanin deposition in the basal cell layer (resembles freckles, but in the mucosa too). Hamartomatous polyps predominantly in the small intestine (especially jejunum). Symptoms: abdominal pain, GI bleeding, intussusception (due to large polyps). Complications: Intussusception (the most common acute presentation in children) GI bleeding → anemia Malignancy risk: GI tract (esp. pancreas), breast, gonadal tumors Management: Symptomatic relief for obstruction/bleeding Endoscopic polypectomy for large polyps Cancer surveillance: colonoscopy, upper GI endoscopy, pancreatic screening Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (Option A) – Hundreds to thousands of adenomatous (not hamartomatous) polyps in the colon, due to APC gene mutation; no mucocutaneous pigmentation. Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (Option C) – Multiple juvenile polyps (hamartomas) in colon/rectum, usually <5 years; no mucocutaneous pigmentation. Cronkhite–Canada Syndrome (Option D) – Non-hereditary, middle-aged adults; GI polyps + alopecia, skin hyperpigmentation, nail atrophy (but not perioral mucosal pigmentation pattern). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A young adult patient presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.stemHtml: A young adult patient presents with a fracture of the neck of the femur. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.solution: trong> The most appropriate management for a femoral neck fracture in a young adult is internal fixation . This method involves surgically inserting screws or a plate to stabilize the fracture while preserving the patient's natural hip joint. Preserving the Femoral Head : Unlike older patients, young adults have a higher potential for the femoral head to heal and maintain its blood supply. Internal fixation is chosen to preserve the native femoral head and joint, which is crucial for a young, active patient. Preventing Complications : The goal is to achieve an accurate reduction and stable fixation to promote healing and reduce the risk of complications such as avascular necrosis (AVN) and nonunion, which are more likely if the fracture is not treated correctly. Incorrect Options: External fixation (Option A) is typically used for temporary stabilization in cases of polytrauma or open fractures but is not the definitive treatment for a femoral neck fracture. Hemiarthroplasty (Option C) involves replacing the femoral head but not the acetabulum. It is primarily reserved for elderly, low-demand patients who are not expected to have a good outcome with internal fixation. Total hip replacement (Option D) involves replacing both the femoral head and the acetabulum. This is the gold standard for treating arthritic hips or for elderly, active patients with displaced femoral neck fractures, but it is generally avoided in young adults to preserve the native joint for as long as possible. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presented to EMT with H/o Penetrating chest trauma. On examination, severe tracheal deviation was present. What is the immediate step of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old male presented to EMT with H/o Penetrating chest trauma. On examination, severe tracheal deviation was present. What is the immediate step of management?
questions.solution: s="customMeta" data-dictid="55b31d659b16927771958a15837b10">penetrating trauma, severe tracheal deviation after chest trauma strongly suggests tension pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency caused by one-way air entry into the pleural space, leading to: Increased intrathoracic pressure → collapse of the ipsilateral lung → pushes mediastinum away from affected side. Mediastinal shift → compression of the opposite lung and major vessels Obstructive shock → ↓ venous return, ↓ cardiac output Do NOT wait for imaging like CXR or E-FAST; immediate decompression is required. Needle decompression → large-bore cannula into the 5th intercostal space (mid-axillary line), followed by ICD (chest tube) placement. Tension Pneumothorax: Causes: Trauma (blunt/penetrating), barotrauma, mechanical ventilation, rib fractures. Symptoms: Sudden respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypotension, unilateral absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and distended neck veins. Management: Immediate needle decompression Intercostal chest drain insertion for definitive management Chest X-ray (Option B) – Imaging delays life-saving intervention; done after stabilizing the patient. E-FAST (Option C) – Bedside ultrasound is useful in trauma, but here the diagnosis is clinical, and urgent treatment is the priority. O₂ support at 100% (Option D) – Oxygen is supportive but will not relieve the life-threatening pressure in the pleural space. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with a ring-shaped (lytic) lesion in the bone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with a ring-shaped (lytic) lesion in the bone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: tomMeta" data-dictid="5618681fbe16927771804370383aaa">abscess is a subacute or chronic form of osteomyelitis , a bacterial infection of the bone. It's most commonly found in the metaphysis of long bones, particularly in the tibia. Imaging Features : On an X-ray, it presents as a lytic, ring-shaped lesion surrounded by a thick, reactive sclerotic rim . The central lytic area represents the pus-filled abscess, while the sclerotic rim is new bone formation laid down by the body in response to the chronic infection. Clinical Presentation : Patients, often young adults, may experience localized pain that is worse at night and relieved by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Incorrect Options: Simple bone cyst (Option B) : This is a benign, fluid-filled lesion that appears as a simple, lucent (lytic) area in the bone, without the characteristic sclerotic rim seen in Brodie's abscess Aneurysmal bone cyst (Option C) : This is a benign, expansile lesion often described as having a "soap bubble" appearance on imaging. It is filled with blood and has a thin shell of bone. It does not typically have the thick, sclerotic rim of a Brodie's abscess. Osteoid osteoma (Option D) : This is a benign bone tumor characterized by a small, radiolucent nidus (the actual tumor) surrounded by a large area of reactive cortical sclerosis. While it has a sclerotic component, the central lytic nidus is typically very small and not ring-shaped. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Explanation: The image shows a soft swelling at the umbilicus in a child, which is characteristic of an Umbilical Hernia . Definition: Protrusion of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring due to incomplete closure of the abdominal wall after birth. Typical presentation in children: Soft bulge at the navel. Prognosis: Most close spontaneously by 2–3 years of age. Spigelian Hernia (Option B): Occurs along the semilunar line (lateral edge of the rectus abdominis muscle), not at the umbilicus. Femoral Hernia (Option D): Appears as swelling below the inguinal ligament , more common in adult females. @Neet_pg_bot

This is an important distinction because the blood supply to the femoral head is typically well-preserved in these fractures, leading to a lower risk of avascular necrosis compared to femoral neck fractures. Pubic rami fracture (Option D) is a type of pelvic fracture and is not a fracture of the femur. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the hospital. Parents report a history of a single fall, but X-ray reveals multiple fractures at different stages of healing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the hospital. Parents report a history of a single fall, but X-ray reveals multiple fractures at different stages of healing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Explanation: This clinical scenario presents a classic case of non-accidental injury, also known as battered baby syndrome or child abuse. The key red flags are: Inconsistent History: The parents' report of a single, minor fall is inconsistent with the severity and number of fractures. A single fall from a short height is highly unlikely to cause multiple fractures in an infant. Multiple Fractures at Different Stages of Healing: The presence of both new fractures and older, healing fractures on the X-ray is a strong indicator of repeated trauma over time, not a single event. Fracture Patterns: Certain fracture patterns are highly suggestive of abuse, such as metaphyseal corner fractures (also known as "bucket handle" fractures) and posterior rib fractures in an infant. Incorrect Options: Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A) is a genetic disorder characterized by brittle bones. While it can cause multiple fractures, it is typically accompanied by other signs, such as blue sclera, a family history of the condition, and a history of fractures from minimal trauma, but not usually from the severe, inconsistent trauma seen in abuse. Accidental fall (Option B) is ruled out by the discrepancy between the reported history and the X-ray findings. A single fall would not explain multiple fractures in different stages of healing. Birth trauma (Option D) could cause an acute fracture, such as a clavicle or long bone fracture, but these fractures would all be at the same, acute stage of healing and would be consistent with the delivery process, not multiple fractures at different stages. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following veins are involved in the formation of esophageal varices?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following veins are involved in the formation of esophageal varices?
questions.solution: sophageal varices occur due to portal hypertension (commonly from liver cirrhosis). In portal hypertension, blood flow is obstructed in the portal vein, leading to the formation of portosystemic anastomoses. One important site is lower esophagus, where: Portal circulation: Left gastric vein (drains into portal vein) Systemic circulation: Esophageal veins (drain into azygos vein → superior vena cava) Increased pressure in the left gastric vein causes dilated submucosal esophageal veins → varices. Right gastric vein (Option B): Drains the lesser curvature of the stomach. It connects to the portal vein, but not a major contributor to lower esophageal varices. Left gastroepiploic vein (Option C): Drains the greater curvature of the stomach into the splenic vein (portal system). It is not involved in esophageal portosystemic anastomosis. Right gastroepiploic vein (Option D): Drains into the superior mesenteric vein (portal system). It has no role in esophageal varices. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Injury to which part causes difficulty in dorsiflexion of the foot?
questions.stemHtml: Injury to which part causes difficulty in dorsiflexion of the foot?
questions.solution: ng> The x-ray shows nerves labelled around the knee. B is pointing to the common peroneal nerve. Function of the Common Peroneal Nerve: The common peroneal nerve is responsible for innervating the muscles of the anterior and lateral compartments of the lower leg. Specifically, it branches into the deep and superficial peroneal nerves. The deep peroneal nerve innervates the tibialis anterior muscle , which is the primary muscle responsible for dorsiflexion of the foot (lifting the foot upward). Clinical Significance: Injury to the common peroneal nerve, which is common due to its superficial location around the fibular head, results in the inability to dorsiflex the foot. This condition is known as foot drop , where the foot hangs down and the patient has to lift their leg high to avoid dragging their toes while walking. Incorrect Options: A- Sciatic nerve (Option A) is the main nerve of the leg. An injury to this nerve would cause much more widespread weakness, affecting both dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, as well as the hamstring muscles. C- Tibial nerve (Option C) innervates the muscles of the posterior compartment of the lower leg, which are responsible for plantarflexion (pointing the foot downward). An injury to this nerve would cause difficulty in plantarflexion. D- Deep peroneal nerve (Option D) is a terminal branch of the common peroneal nerve. While an injury to this specific branch would cause foot drop, the injury at the level of the common peroneal nerve (B) is a more common site of injury. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An elderly woman involved in a road traffic accident presents with difficulty in breathing and altered mental status. D-Dimer is elevated. X-ray findings are suggestive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An elderly woman involved in a road traffic accident presents with difficulty in breathing and altered mental status. D-Dimer is elevated. X-ray findings are suggestive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: strong> The patient's presentation following a road traffic accident is highly suggestive of a fat embolism syndrome. This condition occurs when fat globules from the bone marrow are released into the bloodstream after a long bone fracture, traveling to the lungs and brain. The classic triad of symptoms includes: Respiratory Distress: This is the most common symptom, typically occurring 24-72 hours after the trauma . The fat emboli obstruct the pulmonary capillaries, leading to hypoxia and respiratory failure. The chest X-ray often shows bilateral patchy infiltrates, mimicking acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), as seen in the image provided. Neurologic Changes: These can range from altered mental status to confusion, agitation, and even coma, as the fat emboli affect the cerebral circulation. Petechial Rash: A characteristic, but not always present, rash of tiny red spots on the chest, neck, and axilla is a classic finding. An elevated D-dimer is a non-specific finding that can be seen in both fat embolism and pulmonary embolism, as it indicates a breakdown of a clot. However, the combination of respiratory distress and neurological changes following a long bone fracture (common in road traffic accidents) makes a fat embolism the most likely diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Gas gangrene (Option A) is a severe bacterial infection that would present with crepitus (a crackling sensation under the skin) and a foul-smelling discharge, not the respiratory and neurological symptoms described. Infection (Option C) would typically present with fever and leukocytosis, which are not the primary features of this acute post-traumatic event. Pulmonary embolism (Option D) is a similar condition but lacks the characteristic petechial rash and is less likely to cause the specific neurological changes associated with fat embolism. While a D-dimer would be elevated, the clinical picture points more strongly to fat embolism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with the fracture shown in X-ray. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this type of fracture?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with the fracture shown in X-ray. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this type of fracture?
questions.solution: adial nerve Explanation: The X-ray shows a spiral fracture of the midshaft humerus. This type of fracture is notoriously associated with injury to the radial nerve , which runs in close anatomical proximity to the bone at this specific location. Anatomical Proximity: The radial nerve courses through the spiral groove (or radial groove) on the posterior aspect of the humerus. This close relationship makes it highly vulnerable to trauma during a fracture of the midshaft. Clinical Presentation: An injury to the radial nerve typically presents with wrist drop , which is the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. This is a result of the nerve's innervation of the extensor muscles of the forearm. The incidence of radial nerve palsy in these fractures is approximately 10-20%. Incorrect Options: Median nerve (Option A) is located more medially in the arm and is rarely injured in a midshaft humeral fracture. Ulnar nerve (Option C) runs along the medial epicondyle of the humerus and is most commonly injured in fractures of that region, not the midshaft. Axillary nerve (Option D) is located more proximally, around the surgical neck of the humerus, and is most often injured in proximal humeral fractures or shoulder dislocations. @Neet_pg_bot
